name: Freudenberg, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the district court correctly denied the motion to suppress evidence from the defendant's cell phone because U.S. law enforcement's involvement did not constitute a "joint venture" with Belizean police, and that sufficient evidence supported the convictions for first degree murder, use of a deadly weapon, and tampering with physical evidence.

name: MILLER-LERMAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the public convenience and necessity requirement is facially constitutional under rational basis review, promoting reliable transportation services, and that as-applied challenges were not appropriate for this declaratory judgment action.

name: PAPIK, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while the facial challenge was correctly rejected, there are concerns about whether the public convenience and necessity requirement is being correctly applied in practice, potentially harming consumers by protecting existing providers.

name: HEAVICAN, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court's opinion was fully joined, and separately addressed the Secretary of State's recent change in position regarding the legal sufficiency of the referendum petition.

name: MILLER-LERMAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court's opinion was fully joined, and joined Chief Justice Heavican's separate concurrence.

name: CASSEL
description: Concurred, argued that the initiative did not violate the single subject rule under the natural and necessary test, and other claims were not ripe for review.

name: MILLER-LERMAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the ballot initiative seeks to create a constitutional right to abortion with a singleness of subject and does not violate the single subject rule.

name: MILLER-LERMAN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority failed to distinguish between immune child assault and nonimmune child abuse, and that the State should not be immune from negligence based on non-assault abuse by foster parents, as the statutory exception for assault and battery should not apply to non-state actors.

name: Heavican, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-2292 is constitutional as it falls within the judiciary's sentencing function and does not violate the separation of powers.

name: Cassel, J.
description: Concurred in the result of reversing and remanding but dissented on the constitutionality of the statute, arguing that § 29-2292 is unconstitutional because it delegates executive power to the judiciary.

name: Funke, J.
description: Dissented, joining Justice Papik's dissent and Justice Freudenberg's separate dissent, arguing the statute is unconstitutional.

name: Papik, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-2292 is unconstitutional as it violates the separation of powers by allowing the judiciary to dismiss filed criminal charges without prosecutorial consent or legal/factual insufficiency.

name: Freudenberg, J.
description: Dissented, joining Justice Papik's dissent and arguing that the statute creates a process of judicial clemency that trespasses upon the exclusive executive clemency power, violating the separation of powers.

name: HEAVICAN, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that L.B. 574's provisions on abortion and gender-altering care are germane to the single subject of "public health and welfare" or "regulation of permissible medical care."

name: PAPIK, J.
description: Concurred, argued that L.B. 574 does not violate the single subject rule but suggested that the court should reconsider its precedent on defining "subject" in future cases.

name: MILLER-LERMAN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that abortion and gender-affirming care are not "one subject" and the majority's broad interpretation of "object" or "purpose" is inconsistent with the constitutional text.

name: Stacy, J.
description: Concurred, argued that TERC's conclusion that the County Board had a plain legal duty to equalize by treating irrigated cropland as dryland was factually incorrect, not supported by competent evidence, and failed to conform to the law, as the Mosers failed to prove systematic intentional will or failure of plain legal duty.

name: Cassel, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority incorrectly concluded that an error in subclassification did not trigger a plain duty to equalize, as the Nebraska Constitution compels uniformity across agricultural land classes.

name: Papik, J.
description: Dissented, argued that TERC was required to faithfully apply constitutional principles of uniformity and proportionality, and its decision was supported by competent evidence.

name: Freudenberg, J.
description: Dissented, argued that TERC was required to faithfully apply constitutional principles of uniformity and proportionality, and its decision was supported by competent evidence.
